opus-5.5.text:
I think it's because, if you look at where human intelligence really shows its power, it's mostly not at the level of a single individual. One person, even a very smart one, is actually quite limited. You can only remember so much, think so fast, live so long. But when you put humans together into companies, research labs, governments, open-source communities, something much more powerful comes out of it. Most of the things we're proud of as a civilization, like building a chip fab, sending people to the moon, or running a modern economy, are achievements of organizations, not individuals.

So when I think about AI, especially agents, a natural question is: we've spent a lot of effort making a single model smarter, but what's the analogue of organization for AI? How do you get many agents, or agents and humans together, to collaborate, divide labor, communicate, keep shared memory, and build on each other's work over long time horizons?

Human organizations are interesting because they're basically solutions people have found, through a lot of trial and error, to exactly those problems. Hierarchy, specialization, meetings, documents, incentives, culture: each one is a way to handle limited bandwidth, limited trust, and limited context. Some of these solutions might transfer directly to AI systems, and some might not, because AI has very different constraints. It can copy itself, it can read a million tokens, but it may not have persistent memory or long-term goals in the same way.

So for me it's partly a source of inspiration and partly a mirror. By looking at how humans organize, you understand what the real bottlenecks of intelligence are beyond raw capability. That tells you which problems are worth solving next. I suspect the next big jump in usefulness won't only come from a smarter model. It will come from figuring out the right organizational form for intelligence, whether that's AI with AI or AI with people.

r001.rationale: The response presents organizations as broadly useful ways to combine people’s capabilities and cites varied achievements—chip fabrication, spaceflight, and a modern economy—that they make possible.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes from thinking about agents. When you build an agent, the core question is really: how does a system with limited intelligence and limited context still manage to do something big and complicated? And human organizations are the best existing answer to that question. No single person understands how to build an iPhone or run a country, yet companies and governments do it. That's an extremely interesting phenomenon—intelligence that lives not in any individual, but in the structure connecting them.

So when I look at a company, I see it almost like a multi-agent system. There's a division of labor, there's an interface between roles, there's memory in the form of documents and processes, there's a reward signal in the form of promotions, salaries, and culture. And there are failure modes too—information gets lost between layers, incentives get misaligned, people optimize for the metric instead of the goal. These are exactly the problems we hit when we try to make language models work together or work over long horizons.

Another reason is that I believe the bottleneck for AI right now is shifting. For a long time the question was whether a single model could be smart enough. Now a single model can already do many tasks quite well, but we still don't know how to let many of them, or one of them over a very long time, coordinate to accomplish things at the scale of a real organization. Humans have spent thousands of years iterating on this—from tribes to armies to modern corporations. There's a huge amount of accumulated design wisdom there, and I think it's a bit wasteful not to study it.

And honestly, part of it is personal curiosity. When I moved from a university lab to a company, I noticed that the way people organize themselves changes what kind of research gets done. Same talent, different structure, completely different outcomes. That made me realize organization itself is a kind of technology, and like any technology, it can be understood and improved.

r001.rationale: The response presents human organizations as a way to accomplish large, complex tasks and gives varied examples: building an iPhone and running a country. This communicates their broad, general-purpose value.

astra-6.text:
I find them interesting because an organization is a way of turning individual capabilities into collective capabilities. One person has limited knowledge, limited time, and limited attention. But if you organize many people well, they can accomplish things that none of them could accomplish alone.

The tricky part is that putting more people together doesn’t automatically make the group smarter. You need to divide the work, communicate useful information, make decisions, and correct mistakes. A lot depends on how those processes are designed.

That also makes organizations an interesting lens for thinking about AI. We tend to focus on how capable an individual model is, but there’s another question: how should a system organize its work? What should it handle itself, what should it delegate, and how should it check the results? Human organizations give us a rich set of ways to think about those questions—including examples of what can go wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says organizations help groups accomplish things individuals could not, but it does not clearly characterize them as general-purpose methods for creating many different valuable things.

sol-6.1.text:
I find them interesting because intelligence isn’t only a property of individuals. A group of very smart people can still make poor decisions, while a well-organized group can accomplish things that none of its members could do alone. So the organization itself matters: how information flows, how work gets divided, who makes decisions, and how mistakes get corrected.

That also raises interesting questions for AI. If we have many agents, what should they share? When should they work independently, and when should they coordinate? Human organizations give us ways to think about those questions, including examples of what goes wrong. Adding more people—or more agents—doesn’t automatically make a system more capable. You have to understand the cost of communication and coordination.

r001.rationale: The response says organization helps groups accomplish things members could not do alone, but does not characterize organizational forms as general-purpose methods for creating many different valuable things.
